Runtime: Node.js (serverless or server). Server Actions: server-only functions called from client components.
Best For: Next.js apps — co-located with frontend, no separate server to deploy, simplest setup, built-in routing, easy to start. Server Actions let frontend components call server functions directly (form submissions, data mutations) without a separate API endpoint.
Tradeoffs: Tied to Next.js — not reusable for non-Next.js frontends. Serverless functions can have cold starts (but less of an issue on Vercel with their optimization). Complex backends may outgrow API routes — separate backend may be better for large/complex apps.
Default For: Default for Next.js apps — simplest if you're already using Next.js.

Runtime: Node.js (long-running server process). Can be deployed on a VPS, container (Docker), or platform (Railway, Render, Fly.io, AWS, GCP, etc.).
Best For: Separate backend — independent of frontend, can serve multiple frontends (web, mobile, etc.), more control over server, easier to scale independently, good for complex backends with significant business logic, background jobs, websockets, etc. Mature ecosystem (Express, Fastify, Hono, etc.).
Tradeoffs: More setup — separate server to deploy, manage, monitor. More infrastructure to maintain. More deployment complexity. Overkill for simple apps.
Default For: When you need a separate backend — complex app, multiple frontends, significant business logic, independent scaling, not using Next.js, or want full control over the backend.

Runtime: Python (long-running server process or serverless). FastAPI is async, fast, modern (type hints, automatic OpenAPI docs, dependency injection).
Best For: Python shops, data-heavy apps, ML/AI integrations, apps where Python is the team's strength, apps needing data processing / ML capabilities. FastAPI is modern, fast, well-documented, great for APIs. Django / Flask are alternatives (Django is more full-featured, Flask is lighter).
Tradeoffs: Python runtime, different from JavaScript/TypeScript — different ecosystem, different tooling. Need Python hosting (or serverless Python). Not the default if your team is JavaScript-focused.
Default For: When your team uses Python, your app is data-heavy or needs ML, or you prefer Python for the backend.

Runtime: PHP (long-running server process). Modern PHP with Laravel — elegant syntax, built-in ORM (Eloquent), queue system, authentication, validation, testing, good developer experience. Laravel ecosystem (Forge, Vapor, Nova, etc.).
Best For: PHP shops, teams experienced with Laravel, apps where Laravel's built-in features (auth, queues, ORM, etc.) are valuable, rapid development with a full framework. Laravel is a full-stack framework — batteries included.
Tradeoffs: PHP runtime — different from JavaScript/TypeScript. Different ecosystem. Not the default if your team is JavaScript-focused. Laravel is opinionated — good if you like its conventions, less ideal if you want a minimal setup.
Default For: When your team uses PHP/Laravel, or you want a full-stack framework with batteries included.

Language: TypeScript / JavaScript (or other languages on some platforms)
Runtime: Serverless — functions run on-demand, scale automatically, pay per execution. Vercel: integrates with Next.js, easy to deploy. Cloudflare Workers: edge runtime, very fast, low cost, different runtime (not Node.js — uses Web APIs / Cloudflare-specific APIs).
Best For: Sporadic/low-volume workloads, event-driven tasks, webhooks, scheduled jobs (cron), lightweight APIs, apps where pay-per-use is cost-effective. Vercel functions are easy if you're on Vercel. Cloudflare Workers are very fast and cheap, but use a different runtime (not Node.js — check compatibility).
Tradeoffs: Cold starts (though Vercel optimizes this; Cloudflare Workers have near-zero cold starts). Execution time limits (Vercel: 10s on Hobby, 60s on Pro; Cloudflare: 10ms-30s depending on plan). Not ideal for long-running tasks. Vendor lock-in (Vercel or Cloudflare). Debugging can be harder than a long-running server.
Default For: Sporadic workloads, webhooks, scheduled jobs, lightweight APIs, event-driven tasks. Good for offloading specific tasks from your main backend.

Runtime: Client-side — frontend talks directly to Supabase (PostgreSQL, auth, storage, realtime) via SDK. No separate backend server needed for many use cases.
Best For: Simple apps that want auth + database + storage + realtime without building a backend. Less backend code to write. Good for prototypes, small apps, apps where the BaaS covers your needs. Row-level security (RLS) in PostgreSQL controls data access per user.
Tradeoffs: Less control — you're tied to Supabase's features and limits. Can't implement complex backend logic that doesn't fit Supabase's model. Vendor lock-in (though data is standard PostgreSQL). Security model depends on RLS — must configure RLS correctly to protect data. Not ideal for complex business logic, custom backend processing, integrations that need a server.
Default For: Simple apps, prototypes, apps where auth + database + storage + realtime covers your needs. Good starting point — you can add a separate backend later if you outgrow the BaaS.
